Floating-point addition is not associative because modern hardware represents real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, adding three numbers gives the same result regardless of whether the first two or the last two are added first. In floating-point arithmetic, however, most exact results cannot be represented. After each operation, the hardware rounds the result to the nearest representable value, usually according to the IEEE 754 standard. Changing the order of operations changes which intermediate values are rounded, so it can change the final answer.

The effect is especially visible when numbers have very different magnitudes. If a very small number is added to a very large number, the small contribution may fall below the available precision and disappear entirely. If several small numbers are added together first, their accumulated value may become large enough to affect the later addition. Cancellation between positive and negative values can also amplify rounding effects because the meaningful leading digits cancel, leaving a result whose remaining digits are sensitive to earlier errors.

Large matrix multiplications consist of many dot products. Each output element is formed by multiplying corresponding entries from a row and a column and then summing those products. Although the mathematical sum has no prescribed order, an implementation must choose one. A sequential CPU implementation might accumulate products from left to right, while a vectorized implementation may maintain several partial sums. A multicore CPU or GPU may divide the work into blocks, compute partial results independently, and combine them using a reduction tree. Different thread schedules, block sizes, vector widths, compiler optimizations, or hardware generations can therefore produce different reduction orders.

Fused multiply-add instructions add another source of variation. They compute a multiplication and addition with a single final rounding, whereas separate instructions round the product before adding it. Both approaches are valid, but they need not produce identical bits. Specialized matrix hardware may also use reduced-precision inputs or intermediate accumulators.

Consequently, two mathematically equivalent matrix multiplications can differ slightly in their low-order bits. For well-conditioned calculations, these differences are usually tiny and remain within an expected numerical tolerance. In ill-conditioned problems or long chains of later computations, they can become more noticeable.

Bitwise reproducibility therefore requires more than using the same input data. It generally requires fixing the algorithm, reduction order, thread configuration, compiler behavior, instruction set, and precision rules. Deterministic reduction schemes, higher-precision accumulation, compensated summation, or reproducible numerical libraries can reduce or eliminate variation, but they often impose costs in speed, memory use, or parallel scalability.
